title: Choose between modular monolith and microservices for a new product
description: Evaluate when to deploy a modular monolith versus a microservice architecture for a greenfield product, considering team structure, deployment velocity, and operational complexity.

data.text: You are the first senior engineer at a Series A startup. The product is a project management SaaS with three bounded contexts: **Teams**, **Tasks**, and **Billing**. You have two backend engineers and a three-month runway to a public beta. The CTO has asked whether you should start with microservices or a modular monolith.

terms.definition: A single deployable application with strict internal module boundaries enforced by language visibility rules.
A small, independently deployable service owning its own data and communicating over a network.
A DDD concept: the boundary where a particular domain model applies.
Organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which copy the communication structures of those organizations.
Services that must be deployed together because of tight coupling, combining the costs of both architectures.

data.title: Common trap
data.text: Many teams choose microservices because they assume it is 'more scalable.' It is—only after you have solved the hard problems of distributed systems. Starting with microservices to avoid a problem you do not yet have is a form of premature optimization.

cards.title: Modular Monolith
cards.description: One repository, one deployment unit, strict internal module boundaries.
pros: In-process calls avoid network latency and serialization
Lower operational overhead for a small team

cards.title: Microservices
cards.description: Multiple services, each with its own database and deployment pipeline.
pros: Team autonomy over lifecycle and technology
cons: Network latency, serialization, and partial failure

data.text: Use this checklist before recommending an architecture. The answer should be a concrete recommendation, not 'it depends.' Explain why it depends on what.

items.text: Team size: fewer than 8 engineers strongly favors a monolith.
Domain boundaries: are they stable and well-understood?
Scaling profile: is one context write-heavy relative to others?
Compliance or data residency requirements per context?
CI/CD maturity: can you safely deploy one service ten times per day?
Observability budget: do you have distributed tracing and structured logging today?
Failure modes: can you tolerate partial outages, or do you need atomic transactions?

data.title: The distributed monolith
data.text: If your services share a database schema, require synchronized deployments, and communicate with synchronous RPC, you have built a distributed monolith. You paid the microservices tax and received none of the benefits.

data.title: Recommended approach: Modular Monolith with Strangler Fig preparation
data.content: For a two-engineer team with a three-month beta deadline, a modular monolith is the correct starting point. The reason is not that microservices are bad—it is that their complexity must be earned through team size, traffic volume, or deployment independence requirements that do not yet exist.
data.code:
// Recommended structure
src/
  ProjectManagement/
    Teams/          // Owns Team aggregate
    Tasks/          // Owns Task aggregate
    Billing/        // Owns Invoice aggregate
    SharedKernel/   // Only truly shared types
  Program.cs

// Each module has its own DI registration:
services.AddTeamsModule()
        .AddTasksModule()
        .AddBillingModule();

data.text: Design the monolith so that each bounded context owns its data schema and exposes a public interface. When the team grows past eight engineers or one context requires independent scaling, extract that context into a service using the Strangler Fig pattern: route new requests to the service while keeping the monolith stable.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Start with a modular monolith unless you have a proven need for independent scaling.
Enforce module boundaries with language visibility, not social contracts.
Microservices are a team and organizational solution, not a technical one.
data.takeaway: Choose the simplest architecture that lets you sleep at night—and lets you extract services when the time comes.
